# Generalised additive models

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Generalised additive models";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` humpback whales produce a varied series of sounds for 7 to 30 minutes and then repeat the same series with considerable precision. Payne and McVay called each repeated series a [song]{.hl}.

_Source: Payne & McVay (1971), Science_
:::

## Where we are

So far, every model in this course has been linear in its predictors. Many linguistic data are [curves]{.hl}: formant trajectories, pitch contours, tongue contours, pupil size over a trial, looks to a target over time.

. . .

This lecture and the next one follow Márton Sóskuthy's GAMM workshop (Analysing Curves, University of Manchester, 2018) and his written tutorial (Sóskuthy, 2017), with simulated data and `ggplot2` figures.

## Today

1. Curves
2. Smooth terms
3. Fitting GAMs with `{mgcv}`
4. Comparing curves

## The data {.smaller}

F2 of the PRICE vowel at 11 points (0% to 100% of the vowel), 10 tokens from each of 20 speakers: 10 with English and 10 with Italian as their L1.

```{r}
set.seed(2029)
speakers <- tibble(speaker = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                   l1 = rep(c("English", "Italian"), each = 10),
                   s0 = rnorm(20, 0, 60),
                   s_mid = rnorm(20, 0, 5))
tokens <- crossing(speakers, token = 1:10) |>
  mutate(traj = paste(speaker, token, sep = "."),
         duration = round(runif(n(), 120, 300)),
         t0 = rnorm(n(), 0, 40))
price <- crossing(tokens, time = seq(0, 100, by = 10)) |>
  arrange(traj, time) |>
  mutate(onset = if_else(l1 == "English", 1250, 1320),
         offset = if_else(l1 == "English", 2050, 1900) - 2 * (250 - duration),
         mid = if_else(l1 == "English", 62, 50) + s_mid,
         width = if_else(l1 == "English", 8, 14),
         f2 = onset + (offset - onset) * plogis((time - mid) / width) + s0 + t0) |>
  group_by(traj) |>
  mutate(f2 = round(f2 + as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.6), n = n(), sd = 30)))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(across(c(speaker, l1, traj), factor)) |>
  select(speaker, l1, traj, duration, time, f2)
```

## The data

```{r}
price
```

. . .

What we built in: the glide from [a] to [ɪ] is smaller and earlier for the Italian speakers, short vowels undershoot the glide target, and neighbouring measurements in a token are correlated.

## The trajectories

```{r, fig.height = 2.8}
ggplot(price, aes(x = time, y = f2, group = traj)) +
  geom_line(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ l1) +
  labs(x = "Time (% of vowel duration)", y = "F2 (Hz)")
```

Each line is one token. The research question is whether the two groups produce different F2 trajectories.

# Curves

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` humpback whale song is built in layers. Single sounds ([units]{.hl}) form phrases, a repeated phrase forms a theme, and a fixed sequence of themes forms the song.

_Source: Payne & McVay (1971), Science_
:::

## A straight line

```{r straight-line, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.3}
mean_traj <- price |>
  filter(l1 == "English") |>
  summarise(f2 = mean(f2), .by = time)
m_line <- lm(f2 ~ time, data = mean_traj)
p_fit <- ggplot(mean_traj, aes(time, f2)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(m_line)[1], slope = coef(m_line)[2], colour = pandan, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Mean English trajectory", x = "Time (%)", y = "F2 (Hz)")
p_res <- ggplot(mutate(mean_traj, res = residuals(m_line)), aes(time, res)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = muted, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = vine) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Residuals", x = "Time (%)", y = "Residual (Hz)")
p_fit + p_res
```

The line misses the shape, and the residuals follow a pattern: neighbouring residuals are similar. This is [autocorrelation]{.hl}, and it makes standard errors unreliable.

## Polynomials

```{r polynomials, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.0}
map(c(2, 3, 9), \(d) {
  ggplot(mean_traj, aes(time, f2)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, d), se = FALSE, colour = pandan,
                linewidth = 1.1, n = 200) +
    geom_point(colour = kingfisher, size = 2.5) +
    labs(title = paste("Degree", d), x = "Time (%)", y = if (d == 2) "F2 (Hz)" else NULL)
}) |>
  wrap_plots(nrow = 1)
```

- A quadratic or cubic term [underfits]{.hl}: it cannot follow the flat start and the late rise
- A high-degree polynomial [overfits]{.hl}: it bends to follow the noise

Nothing in the data says which degree to choose.

# Smooth terms

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` humpback whales off eastern Australia replaced their song within two years. A few singers from the west coast had brought a new song, and by 1998 only the [new song]{.hl} was heard.

_Source: Noad et al. (2000), Nature_
:::

## Smooth terms

A generalised additive model can contain [smooth terms]{.hl} next to the usual parametric terms:

<div class="formula">y = α + β₁ · x₁ + f(x₂) + e</div>

`f(x₂)` is a smooth function of `x₂` whose shape is estimated from the data. It is built as a sum of simpler functions, the [basis functions]{.hl}, much as a polynomial is a sum of powers of `x`. A [smoothing penalty]{.hl} keeps it from following the noise.

## Basis functions

```{r basis, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.4}
m_mean <- gam(f2 ~ s(time, bs = "cr", k = 10), data = mean_traj)
grid <- tibble(time = 0:100)
X <- predict(m_mean, newdata = grid, type = "lpmatrix")
basis <- as_tibble(X[, -1]) |>
  mutate(time = grid$time) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "fn", values_to = "value")
weighted <- as_tibble(sweep(X[, -1], 2, coef(m_mean)[-1], `*`)) |>
  mutate(time = grid$time) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "fn", values_to = "value")
p_basis <- ggplot(basis, aes(time, value, group = fn)) +
  geom_line(colour = pandan, linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "9 basis functions", x = "Time (%)", y = NULL)
p_weighted <- ggplot(weighted, aes(time, value, group = fn)) +
  geom_line(colour = pandan, linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(time = grid$time, value = drop(X[, -1] %*% coef(m_mean)[-1])),
            aes(group = NULL), colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.6) +
  labs(title = "Weighted by their coefficients, and their sum", x = "Time (%)", y = NULL)
p_basis + p_weighted
```

Each basis function is multiplied by a coefficient; the sum (salmon), plus the intercept, is the fitted curve. `bs = "cr"` asks for [cubic regression splines]{.hl}, and `k = 10` gives 10 basis functions, one of which is absorbed by the intercept.

## How wiggly?

- `k` sets the maximum wiggliness: how many basis functions the smooth may use
- The [smoothing parameter]{.hl} sets the actual wiggliness: the larger it is, the more wiggliness is penalised
- `{mgcv}` estimates the smoothing parameter from the data, so the strategy is to set `k` high enough and let the penalty do the rest
- The [effective degrees of freedom]{.hl} (edf) describe the result: an edf of 1 is a straight line, and higher values mean more wiggly curves

## The smoothing parameter

```{r penalty, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.6}
sp_hat <- m_mean$sp
fits <- map(c(1e-3, 1, 1e3, 1e6), \(m) {
  mod <- gam(f2 ~ s(time, bs = "cr", k = 10), data = mean_traj, sp = sp_hat * m)
  tibble(mult = m, time = grid$time, fit = as.numeric(predict(mod, grid)), edf = sum(mod$edf) - 1)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(label = paste0(c(`0.001` = "sp / 1000", `1` = "estimated sp",
                          `1000` = "sp × 1000", `1e+06` = "sp × 1e6")[as.character(mult)],
                        " (edf ", round(edf, 1), ")"),
         label = fct_reorder(label, mult))
ggplot(fits, aes(time, fit)) +
  geom_point(data = mean_traj, aes(y = f2), colour = muted, size = 1.8) +
  geom_line(colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Time (%)", y = "F2 (Hz)")
```

The same 10 basis functions with four smoothing parameters. A large penalty pushes the smooth toward a straight line.

# Fitting GAMs with `{mgcv}`

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` over 11 years, [11 song types]{.hl} spread across the humpback whale populations of the South Pacific, usually starting off eastern Australia and reaching French Polynesia within about two years.

_Source: Garland et al. (2011), Current Biology_
:::

## `gam()` and `bam()`

- `{mgcv}` (Wood, 2017) fits GAMs with `gam()`, and with `bam()`, which is much faster on big data sets such as curves
- `s(time)` is a smooth over time; `s(time, by = l1)` fits a separate smooth for each group
- Smooths in a `by` model are centred on zero, so the group difference in height needs its own parametric term, `l1`
- `method = "ML"` is needed to compare models that differ in their fixed effects; the default of `bam()` is `"fREML"`

## A first GAM

```{r}
m1 <- bam(f2 ~ l1 + s(time, by = l1, k = 10), data = price, method = "ML")
round(summary(m1)$p.table, 2)
round(summary(m1)$s.table, 2)
```

## Reading the summary

- The [parametric]{.hl} table works as in `lm()`: the intercept is the mean F2 of the English trajectories, and `l1Italian` is how much higher or lower the Italian trajectories are on average
- The [smooth]{.hl} table has one row per smooth: `edf` close to 9 means a very wiggly curve, close to 1 a straight line


The F test asks whether a smooth is flat, so two identical curves would both come out significant. Testing whether two smooths differ needs a different model, later in this lecture.

## Plotting with `{tidygam}`

```{r, fig.height = 2.8}
m1_pred <- predict_gam(m1, series = "time", length_out = 50)
plot(m1_pred, series = "time", comparison = "l1")
```

`predict_gam()` returns a tibble of predictions with standard errors and 95% confidence intervals; its `plot()` method draws them with `ggplot2`.

## Your own plot {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.0}
ggplot(m1_pred, aes(x = time, y = f2, colour = l1, fill = l1)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci), alpha = 0.3, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Time (% of vowel duration)", y = "Predicted F2 (Hz)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

`m1_pred` is an ordinary tibble with the predictor values, the predicted `f2`, its standard error `se`, and the limits `lower_ci` and `upper_ci`.

## Is `k` high enough?

```{r}
k.check(m1)
```

- `k'` is the number of basis functions available; `edf` is how many the smooth used
- A [k-index]{.hl} below 1 with a small p-value suggests there is pattern left in the residuals that more basis functions could capture


To be sure, raise `k` (for example to 15) and refit. If the curves and the edf barely change, `k` was high enough.

## Choosing `k`

- Start from what you expect: a formant trajectory over 11 points rarely needs more than 10 basis functions; a pitch contour over a whole sentence may need 20 or more
- Look at the fitted curves against the data, compare `edf` with `k'`, and use `k.check()`

. . .

In Sóskuthy's (2018) workshop example, `gam.check()` flagged smooths whose wiggliness simulations showed to be fine. Use these checks as guides, together with the plots.

# Comparing curves

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` in each humpback whale population, only [males]{.hl} sing, and all of them sing the current version of the song, which keeps changing over the years.

_Source: Garland et al. (2011), Current Biology_
:::

## Reference and difference smooths

To test whether two curves differ, the model needs a term for the difference. With an [ordered factor]{.hl} in `by`, `s(time)` becomes the [reference smooth]{.hl} for the first level, and `s(time, by = l1_o)` the difference between the other level and the reference.

```{r}
price <- mutate(price, l1_o = as.ordered(l1))
contrasts(price$l1_o) <- "contr.treatment"
m2 <- bam(f2 ~ l1_o + s(time, k = 10) + s(time, by = l1_o, k = 10),
          data = price, method = "ML")
```

## The difference smooth

```{r}
round(summary(m2)$p.table, 2)
round(summary(m2)$s.table, 2)
```

- `s(time)` is the English trajectory, and `s(time):l1_oItalian` is the [difference smooth]{.hl}: the Italian trajectory minus the English one, apart from the overall difference in height captured by `l1_oItalian`
- `m1` and `m2` fit the same curves in two parametrisations

## Plotting the difference {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 3.0}
m2_diff <- get_difference(m2, "time", list(l1_o = c("Italian", "English")), length_out = 50)
ggplot(m2_diff, aes(x = time, y = diff)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = muted, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci), fill = kingfisher, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Time (% of vowel duration)", y = "Italian − English F2 (Hz)")
```

Where the 95% confidence interval excludes zero, the curves differ. `plot(m2_diff)` shades those stretches automatically.

## Model comparison {.smaller}

```{r}
m2_null <- bam(f2 ~ s(time, k = 10), data = price, method = "ML")
itsadug::compareML(m2_null, m2)
```

The null model drops both the height difference and the difference smooth. Both models are fitted with `method = "ML"`.

## The binary smooth

```{r, eval = FALSE}
price <- mutate(price, is_italian = as.numeric(l1 == "Italian"))
m2_bin <- bam(f2 ~ s(time, k = 10) + s(time, by = is_italian, k = 10),
              data = price, method = "ML")
```

- In a [binary smooth]{.hl}, the `by` variable is numeric (0 or 1), so the smooth is not centred, so a single term covers both the difference in height and the difference in shape
- Its p-value tests both differences at once, which is often the question of interest

## Which test to report?

Sóskuthy's (2018) recommendations:

- Use the model summary only as a rough guide
- Report the significance from a model comparison
- Use prediction plots and the difference smooth for the qualitative discussion: where and how the curves differ

. . .

He calls the binary smooth probably ideal when, as here, a single difference between two curves is the question.

## The catch {.smaller}

These models treat all 2,200 measurements as independent, although 11 come from each token and 110 from each speaker.

```{r, fig.height = 2.3}
tibble(res = residuals(m2), lagged = lag(res), time = price$time) |>
  filter(time > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lagged, y = res)) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "Residual at the previous time point", y = "Residual")
```

Neighbouring residuals are correlated, so the confidence intervals above are too narrow. Lecture 4 deals with this.

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- Polynomials underfit or overfit curves, and leave the choice of degree to the analyst
- A [smooth term]{.hl} is a weighted sum of basis functions; `k` sets the maximum wiggliness and the [smoothing penalty]{.hl} the actual wiggliness
- The smooth table tests whether each smooth is flat; an ordered factor in `by` gives a reference smooth and a [difference smooth]{.hl}; plot the difference with its confidence interval
- Report the significance from a model comparison; describe the curves with prediction plots and the difference smooth
- Models without random effects or an error model are overconfident with curve data
:::
